This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
If $C,D\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ then the distance between $C$ and $D$ is defined by\[\delta(C,D)=\inf_{\substack{c\in C\\ d\in D}}\| c-d\|.\]Let $h(n)$ be the maximal number of unit distances between disjoint convex translates. That is, the maximal $m$ such that there is a compact convex set $C\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ and a set $X$ of size $n$ such that all $(C+x)_{x\in X}$ are disjoint and there are $m$ pairs $x_1,x_2\in X$ such that\[\delta(C+x_1,C+x_2)=1.\]Determine $h(n)$ - in particular, prove that there exists a constant $c>0$ such that $h(n)>n^{1+c}$ for all large $n$.
#956: [ErPa90]
geometry | 
distances | 
convex
A problem of Erdős and Pach [ErPa90], who proved that $h(n) \ll n^{4/3}$. They also consider the related function where we consider $n$ disjoint convex sets (not necessarily translates), for which they give an upper bound of $\ll n^{7/5}$. 
It is trivial that $h(n)\geq f(n)$, where $f(n)$ is the maximal number of unit distances determined by $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (see [90]).

 Good find! This is what GPT-5.5 says about the difference between this preprint of Valtr and the note above: 
Valtr’s preprint contains the core construction, and it should be credited much more prominently. But it does not literally solve Erdős Problem #956 as stated without an extra modification. Valtr proves a very close result: he constructs a strictly convex norm with $\Theta(n^{4/3})$ unit distances, and also an infinite sequence of possibly overlapping translates of one strictly convex centrally symmetric body with $\Omega(n^{4/3})$ touching pairs; he also gives an $O(n^{4/3})$ upper bound for touching pairs among possibly overlapping translates.
The word “possibly overlapping” is the key difference. For the norm ball in Valtr’s construction, those corresponding translates overlap badly. So Valtr’s construction is not, verbatim, an admissible configuration for $h(n)$.
The construction in the note is best described as Valtr’s parabolic-grid mechanism plus a disjointness/unit-distance conversion. It keeps the same parabolic family of difference vectors, but replaces the full norm ball by a very small convex body $D_W$ whose Euclidean unit offset contains the desired parabolic cap.

 It's important to keep in mind that AI is very bad at attribution and this is a core and important problem. What's worse, is AI companies seem to have a vested interest in hiding how AI arrives at answering things to avoid distillation attacks. 
While this lack of attribution makes a particular AI seem 'smarter' it's possible that it is holding back its ability to making meaningful contributions in a broader, more productive manner.
I really applaud people who are contributing more AI proofs, but I think they have a responsibility to work harder on the attribution issue because of that.
